passage: Sea otters spend a large part of each day grooming their fur. Unlike most marine mammals, otters lack a thick layer of blubber, so they rely on air trapped in their dense fur to stay warm in cold ocean water. Regular grooming fluffs the fur and keeps that insulating layer of air in place.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Sea otters spend more time grooming than any other marine mammal does.
Sea otters groom often because their fur, rather than blubber, keeps them warm.
Most marine mammals have stopped relying on fur to stay warm.
Cold ocean water slowly damages the fur of sea otters.
explanation:
Before looking at the choices, try to sum up the text in one sentence of your own. Something like: otters groom a lot because their fur is what keeps them warm.

Every sentence builds toward that. Otters have no blubber, they rely on air trapped in their fur, and grooming keeps that air in place.

Choice B says the same thing: frequent grooming, explained by fur instead of blubber.

rationales.A: The text never compares grooming time with other marine mammals. Watch out for choices that add a comparison the text doesn't make.
rationales.C: The text says most marine mammals have blubber. It never says they stopped relying on fur.
rationales.D: Cold water is why otters need to stay warm. The text never says it damages their fur.

passage:
The following text is from a story. Marisol has recently moved to a small coastal town.

Every morning before school, Marisol walked to the end of the pier. She did not fish, and she did not talk to the old men who did. She simply stood with her hands in her coat pockets and watched the fog lift off the water, counting the boats as they appeared one by one.
stem: According to the text, what does Marisol do at the end of the pier each morning?
choices: She fishes alongside the old men.
She talks with the fishermen about their boats.
She waits for a friend to walk with her to school.
She watches the fog lift and counts the boats.
explanation:
This question asks what the text says, so the answer will be right there in the passage. Find the sentence about what Marisol does.

It says she "watched the fog lift off the water, counting the boats as they appeared one by one." Choice D says exactly that.

Notice how the text also tells you what she does NOT do: she doesn't fish and doesn't talk to the old men. Those details are there to rule out the trap answers.

rationales.A: The text says plainly that she "did not fish."
rationales.B: The text says she "did not talk to the old men" who fish.
rationales.C: No friend appears in the text. She stands on the pier by herself.

passage: In the early 1800s, most towns in the United States kept their own local time, setting their clocks by the position of the sun. As railroads expanded, this patchwork of times made train schedules confusing, since each station along a route might keep a slightly different time. To solve the problem, railroad companies adopted a system of standard time zones in 1883.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Railroad companies adopted standard time zones to end the confusion caused by many different local times.
Towns in the 1800s set their clocks according to railroad schedules.
Trains in the 1800s frequently arrived late because of poorly built tracks.
Local time based on the sun was more accurate than standard time.
explanation:
This text follows a problem and solution pattern, which is very common on the SAT.

Problem: every town kept its own time, so train schedules got confusing. Solution: railroads adopted standard time zones in 1883.

A good main idea covers the whole pattern, not just one half. Choice A includes both the confusion and the fix.

rationales.B: This reverses the order. Towns set their clocks by the sun, and the railroads came later with a shared standard.
rationales.C: Late trains and tracks are never mentioned. The confusion was about schedules and clocks.
rationales.D: The text never says which kind of time was more accurate.

passage: Choreographer Dana Ilves rehearses her dancers in an unusual way: before they learn any steps, she asks them to walk across the studio as they would on a crowded street, a quiet beach, or an icy sidewalk. Ilves argues that ordinary movements carry emotional information that audiences recognize instantly. By building her dances from these everyday gestures rather than from classical ballet positions, she aims to create works that feel familiar even to viewers who have never attended a dance performance.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ilves believes that classical ballet training is unnecessary for professional dancers.
Ilves's dancers find walking exercises more difficult than learning traditional steps.
Ilves builds her dances from everyday movements so that they will feel relatable to a broad audience.
Audiences who rarely attend dance performances prefer works based on classical ballet.
explanation:
The first sentence describes an unusual exercise, but that's just an example. The main idea is the reason behind it.

Ilves builds her dances from ordinary movements because she thinks everyone recognizes them, so even people new to dance will find her work familiar.

Choice C captures both the method (everyday movements) and the purpose (feeling relatable to a wide audience).

Tip: when a text opens with a specific example, look for the bigger point it is there to illustrate.

rationales.A: Ilves chooses not to build her dances from ballet positions, but she never says dancers don't need ballet training.
rationales.B: The text never says how hard the dancers find the walking exercises.
rationales.D: This contradicts the text. Ilves expects everyday gestures to appeal to people who rarely see dance.

passage: Researchers studying a population of desert lizards noticed that the lizards' tails varied greatly in length. To find out why, the team compared lizards from rocky hillsides with lizards from flat, sandy areas. Lizards from the hillsides had noticeably longer tails, which the researchers suggest help the animals keep their balance while leaping between rocks. On the flat sand, where lizards mostly run in straight lines, shorter tails appeared to be no disadvantage.
stem: Based on the text, how do the lizards from flat, sandy areas differ from the lizards from rocky hillsides?
choices: They have shorter tails, which do not seem to put them at a disadvantage in their habitat.
They have longer tails, which help them run in straight lines.
They leap between rocks less successfully because their tails are short.
Their tails vary more in length than the hillside lizards' tails do.
explanation:
The question asks about the sand lizards, but the text describes them partly by comparison with the hillside lizards. So you have to put two details together.

The hillside lizards had "noticeably longer tails," which means the sand lizards had shorter ones. The last sentence says shorter tails "appeared to be no disadvantage" on flat sand.

Choice A combines both: shorter tails, and no disadvantage.

rationales.B: This mixes up the groups. The hillside lizards are the ones with longer tails.
rationales.C: Sand lizards mostly run in straight lines. The text never describes them leaping between rocks.
rationales.D: The text says tails varied across the whole population, not that one group varied more.

passage:
The following text is from a story. Teodor, an elderly clockmaker, is showing his shop to a new apprentice.

Teodor lifted a small brass clock from the shelf and turned it over in his hands. "This one has not kept good time in forty years," he said. "Customers offer to buy it, and I always refuse." He set it down gently by the window, where the light fell on its scratched face. "My father made it for my mother the year they married. Some things we keep for what they remember, not for what they do."
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Teodor is frustrated that he has never been able to repair the brass clock.
Teodor wants the apprentice to learn how to repair old clocks.
Teodor believes that customers undervalue the clocks in his shop.
Teodor keeps the brass clock because of its meaning to his family, not because of its usefulness.
explanation:
In a story excerpt, the main idea often comes through what a character says at the end.

Teodor admits the clock doesn't work and refuses to sell it. Then he explains why: his father made it for his mother. He sums it up himself: "Some things we keep for what they remember, not for what they do."

Choice D restates that line in plain words.

rationales.A: Teodor handles the clock gently and fondly. Nothing suggests he tried and failed to fix it, or that he's frustrated.
rationales.B: He is showing the apprentice around, but the scene is about why he keeps one clock, not about teaching repairs.
rationales.C: Customers actually want to buy the clock. Nothing suggests Teodor thinks they undervalue anything.

passage: For decades, ecologists assumed that lanternfish, small fish that live in the deep ocean, were a minor part of the ocean's food web because few of them were caught in research nets. A newer method, which estimates fish numbers by measuring how sound waves bounce off them, suggests that lanternfish may be far more abundant than net surveys indicated. Researchers using this method propose that lanternfish can sense approaching nets and swim away, so earlier surveys likely undercounted them.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lanternfish are the most abundant fish in the ocean.
A newer counting method suggests that lanternfish are more plentiful than net surveys showed, possibly because the fish avoid nets.
Research nets are no longer useful for studying fish that live in the deep ocean.
Ecologists have concluded that lanternfish play only a minor role in the ocean's food web.
explanation:
This text has a classic shape: an old belief, new evidence against it, and an explanation for the difference.

Old belief: lanternfish are rare, because nets caught few of them. New evidence: sound waves suggest there are many more. Explanation: the fish may sense nets and swim away.

Choice B includes the new finding and the likely reason, and it uses careful words like "suggests" and "possibly," just like the text.

On harder questions, watch for choices that state things more strongly than the text does.

rationales.A: The text says lanternfish "may be far more abundant" than thought. It never claims they are the most abundant fish in the ocean.
rationales.C: The text says nets undercount lanternfish, not that nets are useless for every deep sea fish.
rationales.D: That's the old assumption, the one the new research calls into question.

passage: In a study of nineteenth-century household account books from one rural region, a historian found that many entries recorded not only purchases but also trades: eggs exchanged for thread, a day of sewing exchanged for flour. The historian argues that these records reveal an economy in which money was only one of several ways families obtained goods. She cautions, however, that account books were kept mainly by households that could read and write, so they may not represent every family in the region.
stem: Based on the text, what is the historian's view of the account books?
choices: They show that families in the region rarely used money.
They are unreliable because many of their entries were recorded incorrectly.
They offer useful evidence about how families obtained goods, though they may not reflect every household.
They prove that families who could read and write traded more often than other families did.
explanation:
The historian does two things: she uses the account books as evidence, and then she adds a warning about them. A good answer needs both.

The evidence: trades like eggs for thread show that money was only one way families got goods.

The warning: mostly families who could read and write kept these books, so they may not represent everyone.

Choice C captures the value and the limit together.

rationales.A: She says money was "only one of several ways," which isn't the same as rarely used. This overstates her point.
rationales.B: Her warning is about which families kept the books, not about mistakes in the entries.
rationales.D: The text never compares how often different kinds of families traded.

passage:
The following text is from a story. Ines has returned to her childhood home after many years away.

The kitchen was smaller than Ines remembered, and the yellow paint she had loved as a child had faded to the color of weak tea. Yet when she opened the drawer beside the stove, the same wooden spoons lay inside, arranged exactly as her grandmother had always kept them, largest to smallest. Ines stood there for a long moment, her hand resting on the drawer's edge, before she closed it softly.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although parts of the kitchen have changed, Ines is moved to find something that has stayed exactly the same.
Ines is disappointed that the kitchen no longer matches her memories of it.
Ines decides to repaint the kitchen the yellow color she loved as a child.
Ines realizes that her grandmother kept the kitchen poorly organized.
explanation:
Watch for turning words. The first sentence lists what has changed: the room seems smaller and the paint has faded. Then "Yet" turns the scene toward something that hasn't changed: the spoons, arranged just as her grandmother kept them.

Ines's reaction shows how she feels. She stands still for a long moment and closes the drawer softly. She's moved.

Choice A covers both halves: things changed, but finding something unchanged touches her.

rationales.B: This only covers the first sentence. The word "Yet" shifts the focus to what stayed the same, and that's where the scene lands.
rationales.C: She notices the faded paint, but nothing suggests she plans to repaint.
rationales.D: The spoons are arranged neatly from largest to smallest, which shows careful organization.
